content:
Each new controversy over a cartoon, a film or a burned Quran brings the same charge: Islam punishes criticism with death, and Muslims riot when their Prophet is mocked. The charge mixes scripture, classical law, modern statute and street violence into one picture.

Separating them matters, because each layer answers to a different authority. The Quran is scripture, and its commands bind every Muslim. Classical law is the reasoned work of jurists who disagreed with one another. A modern statute is the act of a particular parliament. Street violence answers to none of these, and the jurists of every school treated a killing carried out by a private person as a crime in its own right. A reader who wants to know what Islam teaches about insults to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ has to look at each layer in turn.

The four points below separate them: what the Quran says about mockery, how the Prophet answered insults, what the classical jurists held, and where the best-known modern blasphemy law comes from.

The Quran expected Muslims to hear insults. It tells them that they will hear much that hurts from those given scripture before them and from the polytheists, and that patience and mindfulness of God are a mark of resolve.[1] When people mock God's verses, believers are told to leave the gathering until the talk turns to something else.[2]

The Prophet himself was told to proclaim his message and turn away from the polytheists, with the assurance that God would suffice him against the mockers.[3] The same scripture forbids Muslims to insult the gods others worship, lest they insult God in ignorance.[4] The instruction is restraint in both directions.

The same note runs through the Meccan chapters, revealed when the insults were daily and the Muslims powerless. The servants of the Merciful are those who, when the ignorant address them, say "peace".[5] The Prophet is told to bear patiently what they say and to leave them with a gracious leaving, and to take what is freely given, command what is right and turn away from the ignorant.[6]

The strongest form of the objection cites two later verses. One says that those who offend God and His Messenger are cursed in this world and the next, and that a humiliating punishment awaits them.[7] The other tells the believers to fight the leaders of disbelief if they break their oaths and attack the religion.[8] The first states a judgement of God and sets no penalty for a court to apply. The second sits in a passage about polytheist tribes who had broken treaties and waged war, and the attack on the religion comes after the broken oath. Neither verse tells an individual to act on his own.

A group of Jews greeted the Prophet with al-samu alaykum, "death be upon you." A'isha answered them in kind. The Prophet told her to be calm, since God loves gentleness in every matter, and replied to the men only with "and upon you."[9]

A'isha reported that after the Prophet was rejected by Ibn Abd Yalil and walked away in distress, the angel of the mountains offered to crush the people between two mountains. The Prophet declined, saying that he hoped God would bring from their descendants people who would worship God alone.[10]

Insults came from inside the community as well. On one campaign, Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, the leader of the hypocrites in Medina, said that when they returned to the city the more honourable would drive out the more humble, meaning the Prophet. The Quran records the remark.[11] Umar asked permission to strike his neck. The Prophet refused, saying, "Leave him, so that people do not say that Muhammad kills his companions."[12] When a man named Dhu al-Khuwaysira told him to his face to be just in dividing the spoils, he answered, "Woe to you, who will be just if I am not?", and again forbade Umar from killing the man.[13]

The strongest form of the objection cites the killing of Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, a chief of the Banu Nadir, after the Prophet asked who would deal with him, and the reports that a few named people were excluded from the amnesty at the conquest of Mecca.[14] Ka'b had gone to Mecca after Badr to mourn the dead of Quraysh and urge them to war against Medina, and the biographers place his killing in that war. The men excluded at Mecca had killed, or betrayed and fled. The jurists who later argued for the death penalty drew on these cases. What they show is a ruler acting in wartime against enemies who combined words with deeds, and they were never treated as a licence for private violence.

The classical schools did treat insulting the Prophet as a grave offence, and critics are right that some jurists prescribed death for it; Mazhar notes a Hanafi report that a Muslim blasphemer is killed without the chance to repent, which he argues is a misreading.[15] The schools differed. Ibn Abidin, the leading Hanafi jurist of the nineteenth century, collected the positions in his treatise on the ruling for one who insults the Prophet. Malik and Ahmad held that a Jew or Christian who insults the Prophet is killed unless he accepts Islam, and al-Shafi'i held that his covenant ends. Abu Hanifa and al-Thawri held that he is not killed, because the polytheism he already holds is the greater wrong, and that he is disciplined and given a discretionary punishment (ta'zir) instead.[15]

Ibn Abidin states that the Hanafi texts and commentaries hold that a dhimmi's covenant is not broken by insulting the Prophet, and records that Ibn al-Humam dissented where the insult is made openly. Later Hanafis disagreed over whether a grave offence could be punished by death as ta'zir at the ruler's discretion, which shows that the school's position is a limit on the penalty, with room for argument at its edge.[15] Arafat Mazhar presents the same school as treating punishment as a matter for the ruler and the court.[16]

The strictest classical position was set out by Ibn Taymiyya in al-Sarim al-Maslul ala Shatim al-Rasul, which argues that one who insults the Prophet is to be put to death whether Muslim or not, and that repentance does not lift the penalty in this world.[17] His book is the main source for the modern hardline view. The Hanafi position recorded by Ibn Abidin is its opposite pole, and the other schools fall between them on questions such as repentance and the status of a non-Muslim.

Every school agreed on one point that the street ignores. A penalty in Islamic law is applied by a court after proof, and the jurists held that a private person who kills someone accused of a capital offence has committed a crime, even if the accusation was true. The procedure exists to protect the accused, and in particular to test the accusation itself. A charge of blasphemy is easy to make and hard to answer, and the court is where the witnesses can be questioned.

The country most cited in this debate is Pakistan. Its blasphemy provisions are rooted in the Indian Penal Code of 1860, drafted under British rule; section 295-A was added by the British in 1927 to restrain tension between Hindus and Muslims, and passed into Pakistani law at partition.[18] Section 295-C, which made derogatory remarks about the Prophet punishable by death or life imprisonment, was added in 1986.[18]

The sections were added in stages under the military rule of Zia ul-Haq. Section 298-A, on derogatory remarks about the family and Companions of the Prophet, came in 1980; section 295-B, on defiling the Quran, in 1982, with life imprisonment; and section 295-C in 1986.[18] In 1990 the Federal Shariat Court ruled that the alternative of life imprisonment in section 295-C was contrary to Islamic injunctions, which left death as the only penalty.[19] The mandatory sentence came from a court ruling in the late twentieth century.

The record of the law since then shows the danger the jurists foresaw. Accusations have often followed disputes over land, business or faith, and people accused, acquitted or merely suspected have been killed by mobs and gunmen. The governor of Punjab, Salmaan Taseer, was shot by his own bodyguard in 2011 for criticising the law. In 2018 the Supreme Court of Pakistan acquitted Asia Bibi, a Christian woman who had spent eight years under sentence of death, finding the evidence against her unreliable.[20] The acquittal followed the classical rule that doubt averts a penalty. The protests against it followed a politics the classical jurists would not have recognised.

The modern statute is therefore a colonial framework extended by a twentieth-century legislature, and its death sentence leaves no room for the discretionary penalty that is the Hanafi starting point for a non-Muslim in Ibn Abidin's account.[15]

The bottom line

The Quran tells Muslims to expect mockery and to meet it with patience, to leave the gathering, and to refrain from insulting what others hold sacred. The Prophet bore personal insults from opponents and from men in his own community, and refused to have them killed. Classical law did treat insult to the Prophet as a grave offence, and the schools disagreed sharply over the penalty, with the Hanafis setting a discretionary punishment for a non-Muslim and Ibn Taymiyya arguing for death. All of them placed the matter in the hands of a court.

The blasphemy code of Pakistan, the example most often cited, grew from a colonial statute, and its mandatory death penalty dates from 1990. Mob violence over an accusation breaks the Quran, the example of the Prophet and the law of every school at once. A reader who meets the charge that Islam kills its critics should ask which of these layers the charge has in mind.
